Spain. A country in southwestern Europe occupying most of the Iberian Peninsula, bordered by Portugal to the west and France to the northeast, with coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. Once the center of a global empire rivaling Britain's, Spain today is the birthplace of Spanish language and culture, a major center of art and literature, and a founding member of the European Union. Its history encompasses Roman occupation, Islamic rule, Christian reconquest, global imperial expansion, and civil conflict.

Spain's geography includes the Pyrenees mountains separating it from France, the sun-baked meseta, the central plateau, and two major coastal regions: the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The Spanish Inquisition from 1478 to 1834, established to maintain Catholic orthodoxy, became notorious for torturing and executing heretics, Jews, and Muslims, becoming a byword for religious intolerance.

The Spanish Empire, beginning with Columbus's voyage in 1492, grew to encompass vast territories in the Americas, making Spain one of the world's most powerful nations from the 16th through 18th centuries. The Reconquista, the centuries-long Christian campaign to reclaim the peninsula from Islamic rule, culminated in 1492 with the fall of Granada. This same year saw the expulsion of Jews and Muslims.

Moorish Spain from 711 to 1492 CE, particularly the Caliphate of Córdoba and the Emirate of Granada, was a center of Islamic civilization, science, and culture that rivaled any in the world. Spain's Golden Age from the 16th to 17th centuries produced literary masterpieces including Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes and plays by Lope de Vega.

The Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 between Republican and Nationalist forces, won by Francisco Franco, served as a rehearsal for World War II and resulted in nearly 500,000 deaths. Spain's museums and architecture, from the Sagrada Familia basilica to the Prado Museum, contain some of Europe's greatest artistic and architectural treasures.
